title: "Decision-Aware Forecasting"
metadata:
  pagetitle: "Decision-Aware Forecasting"
  description-meta: "Why a return forecast trained on mean squared error is trained on the wrong loss, and three corrections in R: shrinking the mean in risk units, acting on fewer forecast dimensions, and tuning on the certainty equivalent."
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
library(tidypm)
library(knitr)
```

Should a return forecaster be trained on mean squared error at all? The
investor who uses the forecast does not pay for its error in squared
percentage points but in the units of the decision it feeds, and
@stoeckl2026means show that for a mean-variance investor those units are
known exactly: the certainty equivalent lost to a forecast error is the error
measured in risk units, so the forecast can be corrected in those units after
the fact, with an intensity that follows from the number of assets and the
length of the sample alone. The general form of the question is the
operations-research one, where @elmachtoub2022 propose training a predictor
on the regret of the decision it induces rather than on its own accuracy;
the finance case is the one in which that regret has a closed form.

This chapter sits on neither side of the horizon axis of
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory: it is about estimation, and the
same corrections apply to a long-run mean and to a conditional one. We first
derive the mismatch between the statistical loss and the decision loss and
three answers to it, then implement each on the sixteen class series in
excess of the bill, scored out of sample from the first month of model year
11, and finally ask which of the three buys most on this market and where
each fails.

```{r}
#| label: data
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return
Re <- R - rf
stopifnot(ncol(Re) == 16L, !anyNA(Re))
N <- ncol(Re); Tn <- nrow(Re); dates <- zoo::index(R)
rf_by_month <- setNames(rf, as.character(dates))
mu <- colMeans(Re); S <- stats::cov(Re)
gamma <- 5
```

## Two Losses for One Forecast {#sec-27-decision-aware-forecasting-theory}

### The statistical loss and the decision loss

Let $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ be the vector of expected excess returns on $N$
assets, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ their covariance matrix, and
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ a forecast of $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ from any source, a
sample mean or the predictive regression of
@sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-theory. A forecaster is trained and judged on
the statistical loss

$$
L_{\text{stat}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}})
= (\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu})'(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu}),
$$ {#eq-27-mse}

the squared error summed over assets. The investor of
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory with risk aversion $\gamma$
maximizes the certainty equivalent
$CE(\boldsymbol{w}) = \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} - \tfrac{\gamma}{2}\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}$,
attains $CE^* = \boldsymbol{\mu}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}/(2\gamma)$
at $\boldsymbol{w}^* = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}/\gamma$, and
holds the plug-in position
$\hat{\boldsymbol{w}} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}/\gamma$
when handed the forecast. Expanding
$CE(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}) = \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}/\gamma - \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}/(2\gamma)$
and subtracting it from $CE^*$ leaves a perfect square:

$$
CE^* - CE(\hat{\boldsymbol{w}})
= \frac{1}{2\gamma}\,
  (\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu})'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu})
= \frac{\text{RAFE}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}})^2}{2\gamma}.
$$ {#eq-27-decision}

The quadratic form is the squared risk-adjusted forecast error of
@salcher2026, and @sec-26-forecast-error-cost-theory derives it and the
bound it places on the Sharpe-ratio gap; we take it from there. In the
language of @elmachtoub2022, @eq-27-decision is the regret of the
mean-variance decision, and their proposal to train on regret instead of on
accuracy is, for this decision, the proposal to train on @eq-27-decision
instead of on @eq-27-mse.

The two losses are quadratic forms in the same error under two metrics, the
identity and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$, and they rank forecasts
differently. In the eigenbasis of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, with eigenvalues
$\lambda_1 \geq \cdots \geq \lambda_N$ and eigenvectors $\boldsymbol{u}_j$, the
error $\boldsymbol{e} = \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \boldsymbol{\mu}$ has
$L_{\text{stat}} = \sum_j (\boldsymbol{u}_j'\boldsymbol{e})^2$ while
$2\gamma$ times the decision loss is
$\sum_j (\boldsymbol{u}_j'\boldsymbol{e})^2/\lambda_j$: the same squared
error costs $\lambda_1/\lambda_N$ times more in the least volatile direction
of the universe than in the most volatile one, and that ratio is the
condition number @sec-07-covariance-matrix-theory measured.

```{r}
#| label: metric
ev <- eigen(S, symmetric = TRUE)
unit_cost <- function(u) as.numeric(t(u) %*% solve(S, u))   # 2 gamma times the decision loss of a unit error
cost_top <- unit_cost(ev$vectors[, 1]); cost_bottom <- unit_cost(ev$vectors[, N])
c(top = cost_top, bottom = cost_bottom, log10_ratio = log10(cost_bottom / cost_top))
```

On the sixteen classes a unit error along the first eigenvector costs
`r sprintf("%.0f", cost_top)` in the units of @eq-27-decision and the same
error along the last costs `r sprintf("%.2g", cost_bottom)`, a ratio of
$10^{`r sprintf("%.1f", log10(cost_bottom / cost_top))`}$. A forecaster that
minimizes @eq-27-mse spends its accuracy where the variance is large; the
optimizer needs it where the variance is small, because
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$ places its largest weights there, the mechanism of
@best1991 in @sec-08-estimation-error-theory. That a forecaster should be
trained on the loss its user bears is an old point [@granger1969;
@elliott2008]; the mean-variance case adds that the loss is known in closed
form. A forecaster trained on
@eq-27-mse can be reconciled with a decision scored by @eq-27-decision in
three places: after the forecast, by correcting its output in risk units and
leaving the model alone, the post-optimal moment correction of
@stoeckl2026means; between forecast and decision, by acting on fewer of its
dimensions, which @salcher2026less price; and inside the training loop, by
replacing the loss with the certainty equivalent of the portfolio the
forecast implies, the parametric policy of
@sec-18-parametric-policies-theory taken one step further.

### Correcting the mean in risk units

Take the setting of @kan2007: excess returns independent
$\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ over $T \geq N + 1$
months, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ the sample mean and
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$ the unbiased sample covariance matrix, so that
$(T-1)\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$ is Wishart and independent of
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$. In risk units, with
$\boldsymbol{m} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and
$\hat{\boldsymbol{m}} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$, the
forecast is $\hat{\boldsymbol{m}} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{m}, \boldsymbol{I}/T)$
and its risk, the expected squared RAFE, is the trace of that covariance:

$$
\mathbb{E}\,\text{RAFE}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}})^2 = \frac{N}{T}.
$$ {#eq-27-price}

Each of the $N$ dimensions costs $1/T$, the variance of an estimated Sharpe
ratio, whatever signal it carries; this $N/T$ is what inflates the promised
Sharpe ratio in @eq-08-inflation.

The correction is Stein estimation in these units. Fix a target in advance
as $\boldsymbol{P}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ with $\boldsymbol{P}$ idempotent of
rank $r$; the two targets used here are zero, $\boldsymbol{P} = \boldsymbol{0}$,
and the grand mean, $\boldsymbol{P} = \boldsymbol{\iota}\boldsymbol{\iota}'/N$,
$\boldsymbol{P}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} = \bar{\mu}\boldsymbol{\iota}$ with
$\bar{\mu}$ the average of the sixteen sample means. Whiten the forecast with
any square root of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}$, shrink its residual from
the target by a James-Stein factor, and map back. @stoeckl2026means show that
the square root cancels and the estimated covariance matrix enters through one
scalar, the sample Mahalanobis length of the residual:

$$
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c
= \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \frac{c}{T}\,\frac{(\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{P})\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}{\hat{q}},
\qquad
\hat{q} = \big((\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{P})\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\big)'\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\big((\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{P})\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\big).
$$ {#eq-27-corrector}

For the grand mean this reads
$\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c = \bar{\mu}\boldsymbol{\iota} + \big(1 - c/(T\hat{q})\big)(\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} - \bar{\mu}\boldsymbol{\iota})$:
the deviation of each sample mean from the average is scaled down by a factor
that depends on how long that deviation is in estimated risk units. The
risk follows from two facts. First, with $q$ the same quadratic form under
the true $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, the ratio $\psi = q/\hat{q}$ satisfies
$(T-1)\psi \sim \chi^2_{T-N}$ and is independent of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$,
a property of the Wishart distribution, so the feasible corrector is the
oracle corrector with its constant randomly rescaled to $c\psi$. Second,
conditional on $\psi$, the identity of @stein1981 turns the cross term between
the error and the shrinkage direction into the divergence of that direction,
which for an idempotent
$\boldsymbol{R} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}(\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{P})\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{1/2}$
is $(\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol{R} - 2)/\|\boldsymbol{R}\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}\|^2$
with $\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol{R} = N - r$. Taking the expectation over
$\psi$ gives the exact risk,

$$
\mathbb{E}\,\text{RAFE}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_c)^2
= \frac{N}{T} - \frac{\tau_P}{T^2}\Big[2c\,(N - r - 2)\,\mathbb{E}\psi - c^2\,\mathbb{E}\psi^2\Big],
\quad
\mathbb{E}\psi = \frac{T-N}{T-1},\;
\mathbb{E}\psi^2 = \frac{(T-N)(T-N+2)}{(T-1)^2},
$$ {#eq-27-risk}

where $\tau_P = \mathbb{E}\|\boldsymbol{R}\hat{\boldsymbol{m}}\|^{-2}$ is
finite whenever $N - r \geq 3$. Everything about
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$ that matters is in the two moments of $\psi$, and
they depend on $N$ and $T$ only. The bracket is a concave quadratic in $c$,
positive on $0 < c < 2(N-r-2)(T-1)/(T-N+2)$ and largest at

$$
c_f = (N - r - 2)\,\frac{T-1}{T-N+2},
$$ {#eq-27-constant}

a function of $N$, $T$ and the target's rank alone: no tuning, no
validation window. It exceeds the oracle constant $N - r - 2$
because $\psi$ has mean below one, so the feasible corrector shrinks less at
the same $c$. For the grand mean the risk is below $N/T$ for every
$N \geq 4$ and $T \geq N + 1$: the corrected mean dominates the sample mean,
the input of every plug-in rule in this book, whenever the sample is longer
than the number of assets.

The lineage matters because the result is easy to mistake for an old one.
@stein1956 showed that the sample mean of three or more normal means is
inadmissible; @james1961 gave the estimator and, for an unknown covariance
matrix, the constant $(N-2)/(T-N+2)$, which is @eq-27-constant with $r = 0$
divided by $T - 1$; @efron1975 moved the target to the grand mean; and
@jorion1986 brought the idea into portfolio choice as the Bayes-Stein
estimator of @sec-06-expected-returns-theory, whose target is the expected
return of the minimum-variance portfolio. What @eq-27-risk adds is that the
target projection need not be orthogonal in risk units: the grand mean's
is symmetric only if $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{\iota} \propto \boldsymbol{\iota}$,
which no covariance matrix with a
`r sprintf("%.1f", max(apply(Re, 2, stats::sd)) / min(apply(Re, 2, stats::sd)))`-fold
spread of volatilities comes near, and the proof uses only
$\boldsymbol{R}^2 = \boldsymbol{R}$ and $\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol{R} = N - r$.
The Bayes-Stein target depends on $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$, and the
theorem does not cover it. Two further things it says. The zero target
rescales the forecast and leaves the direction of the plug-in position
unchanged, so its gain is in the certainty equivalent and not in the Sharpe
ratio; a target of rank one moves the direction. And the theorem ranks the
corrected mean against the sample mean, not against rules that use no mean,
such as $1/N$ or minimum variance, whose gap to the optimum is a population
quantity rather than an estimation error.

### Using less of the forecast

The second answer keeps the forecast and acts on fewer of its dimensions.
@salcher2026less start from the same identity. With
$\boldsymbol{a} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\mu}$ the truth in
risk units and $\hat{\boldsymbol{b}} = \boldsymbol{a} + \boldsymbol{\eta}$ the
forecast, an investor who acts only on the projection
$\boldsymbol{Q}\hat{\boldsymbol{b}}$ onto a $k$-dimensional subspace loses
$\|(\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{Q})\boldsymbol{a}\|^2 + \|\boldsymbol{Q}\boldsymbol{\eta}\|^2$
on every path, because the cross term carries
$(\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{Q})\boldsymbol{Q} = \boldsymbol{0}$; in
expectation, with the isotropic error of the sample mean,

$$
2\gamma\,\mathbb{E}[\text{loss}]
= \underbrace{\|(\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{Q})\boldsymbol{a}\|^2}_{\text{signal discarded}}
+ \underbrace{\frac{k}{T}}_{\text{noise retained}} .
$$ {#eq-27-hard}

A dimension is worth acting on if and only if its squared Sharpe ratio
exceeds $1/T$, the squared standard error of an estimated Sharpe ratio
[@jobson1981; @lo2002]. Shrinkage of the kind in @eq-27-corrector, or the
two-fund scalar of @kan2007 and the combination with $1/N$ of @tu2011, is a
soft reduction: it pays the price on every one of the $N$ dimensions whether
or not the dimension carries signal, and loses to a hard reduction whenever
the signal is concentrated on a few. The familiar rules are fixed cells of
the grid spanned by the number of covariance dimensions estimated and the
number of forecast dimensions acted on: the plug-in rule of
@sec-08-estimation-error-theory keeps $N$ and $N$, minimum variance the
level alone inside a basis of $N$, $1/N$ of @demiguel2009 one and one, the
decile sort of @fama1993 the sign of the ranking and no covariance matrix,
the parametric tilt of @brandt2009 a slope inside a basis of two, and
covariance shrinkage [@ledoit2004] every forecast dimension with the other
side reduced. None sets its granularity from what the forecast can deliver.

The cell that moves does. Order the assets by the forecast, let $\rho$ be
the cross-sectional rank correlation between the forecast and the next
month's return in risk units, the information coefficient of @grinold1989,
and suppose the true profile is linear in the rank. Then the slope of that
profile in risk units is $\tau^2 = \rho^2/(1 - \rho^2)$, cutting the ranking
into $G$ equal groups and acting on the group averages discards about
$N\tau^2/G^2$ of signal and retains $G/T$ of noise, and the loss is minimized
at

$$
G^* = \left(\frac{2\,N\,T\,\rho^2}{1 - \rho^2}\right)^{1/3}.
$$ {#eq-27-groups}

The cube root is the rate @cattaneo2020 derive for the number of
characteristic-sorted portfolios, but the price per
group here is $1/T$ regardless of how many assets the group averages, because
averaging lowers the noise of a portfolio's mean and its risk in the same
proportion; $G^*$ is therefore small, and it falls to one group, which is
$1/N$, when the forecast cannot rank.

### The decision loss inside the training loop

The third answer changes the loss the forecaster is trained on. Let
$f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t)$ be a forecaster with parameters
$\boldsymbol{\theta}$ and conditioning variables $\boldsymbol{x}_t$, and let
$\boldsymbol{w}(\cdot)$ be the map from a forecast to a weight vector: the
plug-in map, or the clipped tilt of @eq-16-tilt. The decision-aware
estimator maximizes the sample certainty equivalent of the portfolio the
forecast implies,

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
= \arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\;
\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t}\Big[r_{p,t+1}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) - \frac{\gamma}{2}\,r_{p,t+1}(\boldsymbol{\theta})^2\Big],
\qquad
r_{p,t+1}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \boldsymbol{w}\big(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t)\big)'\boldsymbol{r}_{t+1},
$$ {#eq-27-loop}

and the parametric policy of @brandt2009 in @eq-18-estimator is the special
case in which the forecast is the weight itself, $\boldsymbol{w}(f) = f$;
@bertsimas2020 call this prescriptive rather than predictive analytics, and
@elmachtoub2022 give the loss its name. The connection to the first answer is
exact in one case. With the plug-in map, a known $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ and
$\boldsymbol{r}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_t + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{t+1}$,
the expected certainty equivalent of month $t$ is
$[\boldsymbol{\mu}_t'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_t - (f_t - \boldsymbol{\mu}_t)'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(f_t - \boldsymbol{\mu}_t)]/(2\gamma)$
by the algebra of @eq-27-decision, so that

$$
\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\;\mathbb{E}\,CE
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\;\mathbb{E}\,\big(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t) - \boldsymbol{\mu}_t\big)'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\big(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_t) - \boldsymbol{\mu}_t\big):
$$ {#eq-27-gls}

the decision-trained forecaster is the least-squares forecaster with its
errors reweighted by $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$, generalized least squares in
the metric the optimizer uses. That is also why the third answer generalizes
beyond mean-variance: nothing in @eq-27-loop uses the quadratic form. Replace
the certainty equivalent by any utility, the plug-in map by any map with
clipping, constraints or costs, and the forecaster by any model of @gu2020,
and only the closed form of @eq-27-gls is lost.

What is also lost is precision. A certainty equivalent realized over $T$
months carries the noise of a Sharpe ratio, whose standard error is of order
$\sqrt{(1 + SR^2/2)/T}$ [@lo2002], and a tuning parameter chosen by that
criterion is a further estimated quantity whose cost none of the displays
above contains; @salcher2026less make the same point for a number of
groups chosen from the window. Each answer therefore comes with the condition
under which it does not help. The correction of @eq-27-corrector drops every
deviation from the target when $c_f \geq T\hat{q}$, which happens when $T$ is
small relative to $N$; the corrected mean is then the grand mean, the
tangency rule becomes minimum variance, and the correction cannot do better
than a rule that never looked at the mean. The rule of @eq-27-groups returns
one group when the forecast cannot rank, and buys nothing when the forecast's
cross-sectional content is small to begin with. And the loop of @eq-27-loop
can choose worse on both counts when the certainty equivalent it tunes on is
noisier than the gain it chases. One of the three partially falsifies its own
prediction on this market, and the implementation says which.

## Three Corrections on Sixteen Classes {#sec-27-decision-aware-forecasting-implementation}

### The corrected mean in a few lines

@eq-27-corrector and @eq-27-constant are a function of
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$, $N$, $T$ and the
target, with the positive part of the factor taken as implementations do.

```{r}
#| label: correct-mean
correct_mean <- function(R, target = c("grand", "zero"), c = NULL) {
  target <- match.arg(target)
  X <- zoo::coredata(R); T <- nrow(X); N <- ncol(X)
  mu <- colMeans(X); S <- stats::cov(X)
  r   <- if (target == "grand") 1L else 0L                 # rank of the target projection
  Pmu <- if (target == "grand") rep(mean(mu), N) else rep(0, N)
  d   <- mu - Pmu                                          # (I - P) mu_hat
  q   <- as.numeric(t(d) %*% solve(S, d))                  # its length in estimated risk units
  if (is.null(c)) c <- (N - r - 2) * (T - 1) / (T - N + 2) # c_f of @eq-27-constant
  h   <- max(1 - c / (T * q), 0)                           # the James-Stein factor, positive part
  list(mu = setNames(Pmu + h * d, colnames(X)), factor = h, c = c, q = q, N = N, T = T)
}

cm_full <- correct_mean(Re)
round(c(c_f = cm_full$c, Tq = cm_full$T * cm_full$q, factor = cm_full$factor), 4)
```

On the full sample of `r Tn` months, @eq-27-constant with $N = `r N`$ and
$r = 1$ is

$$
c_f = (`r N` - 1 - 2)\,\frac{`r Tn - 1`}{`r Tn - N + 2`} = `r sprintf("%.2f", cm_full$c)`,
\qquad
1 - \frac{c_f}{T\hat{q}} = 1 - \frac{`r sprintf("%.2f", cm_full$c)`}{`r sprintf("%.2f", cm_full$T * cm_full$q)`} = `r sprintf("%.3f", cm_full$factor)`,
$$

so that even on thirty-one model years the deviation of each sample mean from
the grand mean is kept at `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cm_full$factor)` of its
size. The Bayes-Stein estimator of @sec-06-expected-returns-implementation is
the natural comparison and is copied here unchanged.

```{r}
#| label: bayes-stein
bayes_stein <- function(R) {
  X <- zoo::coredata(R); T <- nrow(X); N <- ncol(X)
  mu   <- colMeans(X)
  S    <- stats::cov(X) * (T - 1) / (T - N - 2)   # Jorion's unbiased scaling
  Sinv <- solve(S); iota <- rep(1, N)
  mu0  <- as.numeric(t(iota) %*% Sinv %*% mu) / as.numeric(t(iota) %*% Sinv %*% iota)
  d    <- mu - mu0
  v    <- (N + 2) / ((N + 2) + T * as.numeric(t(d) %*% Sinv %*% d))
  list(mu = setNames((1 - v) * mu + v * mu0, colnames(X)), mu0 = mu0, v = v)
}
bs_full <- bayes_stein(Re)
```

Bayes-Stein shrinks `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * bs_full$v)` of the way toward
the minimum-variance mean, the corrected mean
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (1 - cm_full$factor))` of the way toward the grand
mean, and only the second has the exact risk of @eq-27-risk behind it;
exercise 2 checks it by simulation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-27-intensity
#| tbl-cap: "The constant of @eq-27-constant for sixteen classes and four window lengths, its ratio to the oracle constant N - 3, and the factor of @eq-27-corrector averaged over every window of that length, with the share of windows on which the positive part binds."
#| echo: false
pct <- function(x, d = 2) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x)
num <- function(x, d = 3) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x)
intensity <- lapply(c(36L, 60L, 120L, Tn), function(T) {
  ends <- seq.int(T, Tn)
  h <- vapply(ends, function(e) correct_mean(Re[(e - T + 1L):e, ])$factor, numeric(1))
  tibble::tibble(T = T, c_f = (N - 3) * (T - 1) / (T - N + 2), ratio = (T - 1) / (T - N + 2),
                 factor = mean(h), at_zero = mean(h == 0))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
stopifnot(all(diff(intensity$c_f) < 0), all(intensity$factor < 0.5))
at_T <- function(T, col) intensity[[col]][intensity$T == T]

intensity |>
  dplyr::transmute(T, num(c_f, 2), num(ratio, 2), num(factor, 2), pct(at_zero, 0)) |>
  kable(align = "rrrrr", col.names = c("T", "c_f", "c_f / (N - 3)", "mean factor", "factor at zero"))
```

The constant falls with $T$ toward the oracle value $N - 3 = `r N - 3`$, and
at $T = 36$ it is `r sprintf("%.2f", at_T(36L, "ratio"))` times that value:
the shorter the window, the further $\psi$ sits below one. The factor
applied in practice is small at every window, between
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(intensity$factor))` and
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(intensity$factor))` on average, and on
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * at_T(60L, "at_zero"))` of the sixty-month windows
the positive part binds and every deviation from the grand mean is removed.

### Four means in the tangency rule

The correction is scored where @sec-08-estimation-error-implementation scored
the sample mean: the long-only tangency portfolio on rolling windows, as the
quadratic program of that chapter, so that the register of
@sec-25-backtesting-application is reproduced, with the same estimated
covariance matrix for every mean.

```{r}
#| label: qp-rules
gmv_qp <- function(S) {
  n <- ncol(S)
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S * 1e4, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(rep(1, n), diag(n)), bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(w / sum(w), colnames(S))
}
tan_qp <- function(mu, S) {
  n <- length(mu)
  if (max(mu) <= 0) return(structure(gmv_qp(S), fallback = TRUE))
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S * 1e4, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(mu * 1e2, diag(n)), bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  y <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  structure(setNames(y / sum(y), names(mu)), fallback = FALSE)
}
# The register's Sharpe ratio: compounded, in excess of the bill. The certainty
# equivalent is annualized from monthly excess returns at the chapter's gamma.
sharpe_realized <- function(r, rf) {
  n <- length(r)
  (prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - prod(1 + rf)^(12 / n)) / (stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12))
}
ce_annual <- function(e) 12 * mean(e) - gamma / 2 * 12 * stats::var(e)

oos <- seq.int(121L, Tn)                        # the months the register scores
stopifnot(model_year(dates[oos[1]]) == 11L, model_year(dates[120]) == 10L)
```

Each window supplies five fully invested rules: the tangency portfolio on
the sample mean, on Bayes-Stein and on the corrected mean, equal weighting
and minimum variance. One assertion inside the loop states the theory's
claim about the zero target: its unconstrained position is a scalar multiple
of the sample mean's in every window, so the long-only tangency rule, which
is invariant to that scalar, cannot see it.

```{r}
#| label: rolling-means
run_rules <- function(win) {
  lapply(oos, function(m) {
    X  <- Re[(m - win):(m - 1L), ]
    Xm <- zoo::coredata(X); V <- stats::cov(Xm); mh <- colMeans(Xm)
    cm_g <- correct_mean(X, "grand"); cm_0 <- correct_mean(X, "zero"); bs <- bayes_stein(X)
    stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(solve(V, cm_0$mu), cm_0$factor * solve(V, mh))))   # same direction
    means <- list(sample = mh, bayes_stein = bs$mu, corrected = cm_g$mu)
    rules <- c(lapply(means, tan_qp, S = V),
               list(equal_weight = setNames(rep(1 / N, N), colnames(Re)), min_variance = gmv_qp(V)))
    stopifnot(all(vapply(rules, function(w) identical(names(w), colnames(Re)), logical(1))))
    tibble::tibble(
      date = dates[m], rule = names(rules), factor = cm_g$factor,
      total  = vapply(rules, function(w) sum(w * zoo::coredata(R)[m, ]), numeric(1)),
      excess = vapply(rules, function(w) sum(w * zoo::coredata(Re)[m, ]), numeric(1)))
  }) |> dplyr::bind_rows() |> dplyr::mutate(window = win)
}
roll <- dplyr::bind_rows(run_rules(60L), run_rules(120L))

res_means <- roll |>
  dplyr::group_by(window, rule) |>
  dplyr::summarise(sharpe = sharpe_realized(total, rf_by_month[as.character(date)]),
                   ce = ce_annual(excess), vol = stats::sd(excess) * sqrt(12), .groups = "drop")

# The register: tangency and equal weight to the fourth decimal, minimum variance
# within a few thousandths (the register fits it on total returns).
sweep_all <- utils::read.csv("output/tables/oos-sweep.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(universe == "classes", frequency == "months", basis == "gross")
sr_register <- function(s, w) sweep_all$sharpe[sweep_all$strategy == s & sweep_all$window == w]
g_m <- function(rule, w, col = "sharpe") res_means[[col]][res_means$rule == rule & res_means$window == w]
for (w in c(60L, 120L)) stopifnot(
  abs(g_m("sample", w) - sr_register("max_sharpe", w)) < 5e-5,
  abs(g_m("equal_weight", w) - sr_register("equal_weight", w)) < 5e-5,
  abs(g_m("min_variance", w) - sr_register("min_variance", w)) < 5e-3)
```

```{r}
#| label: means-facts
#| include: false
share_gmv <- function(w) mean(roll$factor[roll$window == w & roll$rule == "sample"] == 0)
for (w in c(60L, 120L)) stopifnot(
  g_m("corrected", w) > g_m("bayes_stein", w), g_m("bayes_stein", w) > g_m("sample", w),
  g_m("corrected", w) < g_m("min_variance", w),
  g_m("equal_weight", w, "ce") > g_m("corrected", w, "ce"))
se_sr <- sqrt((1 + (g_m("equal_weight", 60L) / sqrt(12))^2 / 2) / length(oos)) * sqrt(12)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-27-means
#| tbl-cap: "The long-only tangency rule on three estimates of the mean, with equal weighting and minimum variance beside them, on sixty- and 120-month windows over the register's months. The Sharpe ratio is the register's; the certainty equivalent is annual at gamma = 5, gross of costs."
#| echo: false
lab_full <- c(sample = "tangency, sample mean", bayes_stein = "tangency, Bayes-Stein",
              corrected = "tangency, corrected mean", equal_weight = "equal weight",
              min_variance = "minimum variance")
res_means |>
  dplyr::mutate(rule = factor(lab_full[rule], levels = lab_full)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(rule, window, sharpe = num(sharpe), ce = pct(ce), vol = pct(vol, 1)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = window, values_from = c(sharpe, ce, vol)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(rule) |>
  dplyr::select(rule, dplyr::ends_with("_60"), dplyr::ends_with("_120")) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrrr",
        col.names = c("", "Sharpe, 60", "CE, 60", "vol, 60", "Sharpe, 120", "CE, 120", "vol, 120"))
```

Down the Sharpe columns of @tbl-27-means the correction works as a
direction: on sixty-month windows the tangency portfolio earns
`r sprintf("%.3f", g_m("sample", 60L))` on the sample mean, the register's
figure, `r sprintf("%.3f", g_m("bayes_stein", 60L))` on Bayes-Stein and
`r sprintf("%.3f", g_m("corrected", 60L))` on the corrected mean, and on 120
months `r sprintf("%.3f", g_m("sample", 120L))`,
`r sprintf("%.3f", g_m("bayes_stein", 120L))` and
`r sprintf("%.3f", g_m("corrected", 120L))`; the assertions above would fail
the render if the order did not hold at both windows. What the corrected
mean converges to is in the last row: it stays below minimum variance's
`r sprintf("%.3f", g_m("min_variance", 60L))` and
`r sprintf("%.3f", g_m("min_variance", 120L))`, and on
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * share_gmv(60L))` of the sixty-month windows and
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * share_gmv(120L))` of the 120-month ones it *is*
minimum variance, because the factor is zero and a tangency portfolio on a
constant mean is @eq-09-gmv; the theorem ranks the corrected mean against the
sample mean and says nothing about a rule that never estimated one.

Across the certainty-equivalent columns the ranking changes, and the reason
is the length rather than the direction. Equal weighting has the highest
certainty equivalent of the five at both windows,
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * g_m("equal_weight", 60L, "ce"))` against
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * g_m("corrected", 60L, "ce"))` for the corrected
tangency at sixty months, because a fully invested tangency portfolio with a
volatility of `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * g_m("corrected", 60L, "vol"))` is
far below the risk an investor with $\gamma = `r gamma`$ would choose, and
the certainty equivalent charges for that while the Sharpe ratio cannot see
it. The unconstrained position that @eq-27-risk prices, whose length is its
own choice, is left to exercise 1: the correction lowers its
certainty-equivalent loss and leaves the covariance channel of @eq-08-kz
untouched.

### Granularity on the term-spread tilt

The second answer needs a forecast with a cross-section, and the one forecast
in @sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-application that survived out of sample is
the term spread, rebuilt here exactly as there: the US slope read off the
weekly curve at each month end, lagged once, and an expanding regression of
each series' excess return on it from the first month of model year 11. The
other six predictors of that chapter's elastic net are built beside it for
the third answer.

```{r}
#| label: term-forecast
cv <- sim_curve_weekly |>
  dplyr::filter(series %in% c("US_Level", "US_Slope", "US_IG_Spread", "US_HY_Spread")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = series, values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
i_last <- findInterval(dates, cv$date)
stopifnot(all(cv$date[i_last] <= dates), all(dates - cv$date[i_last] < 8))
curve <- xts::xts(cbind(level = cv$US_Level[i_last], term = -cv$US_Slope[i_last],
                        ig = 100 * cv$US_IG_Spread[i_last], hy = 100 * cv$US_HY_Spread[i_last]),
                  order.by = dates)
P    <- cumprod(1 + R)
mom  <- xts::lag.xts(P, 1) / xts::lag.xts(P, 12) - 1
turb <- uncertaintymeasures::OSturbulence(R, rolling = TRUE, roll.obs = 60)$turb
colnames(turb) <- "turb"
common <- merge(curve, turb); stopifnot(identical(zoo::index(common), dates))
common_lag <- xts::lag.xts(common, 1); mom_lag <- xts::lag.xts(mom, 1); rev_lag <- xts::lag.xts(Re, 1)
pairs_of <- function(s) {
  data.frame(date = dates, y = as.numeric(Re[, s]), mom = as.numeric(mom_lag[, s]),
             rev = as.numeric(rev_lag[, s]), zoo::coredata(common_lag))
}
ols_fc <- function(d, v, m) {
  tr <- which(!is.na(d[[v]]) & seq_len(nrow(d)) < m)
  b  <- stats::lm.fit(cbind(1, d[[v]][tr]), d$y[tr])$coefficients
  unname(b[1] + b[2] * d[[v]][m])
}
F_term <- vapply(colnames(Re), function(s) {
  d <- pairs_of(s); vapply(oos, function(m) ols_fc(d, "term", m), numeric(1))
}, numeric(length(oos)))
dimnames(F_term) <- list(as.character(dates[oos]), colnames(Re))
stopifnot(!anyNA(F_term))
```

The forecast becomes a weight through the tilt of @eq-16-tilt, with the same
band $\delta = 1/(2N)$ and scale, and the reduction is inserted where
@eq-27-hard says it belongs: after the forecast has been put into volatility
units and demeaned, before it is clipped. Four cells come from one function:
every magnitude is chapter 16's tilt; three rank groups replaces each
forecast by the average of its tercile; the sign keeps top minus bottom at
the largest tilt the band allows, the long-short sort of @fama1993 around the
policy; equal weighting discards the forecast.

```{r}
#| label: tilt
vol60 <- zoo::rollapply(Re, 60, stats::sd, align = "right", fill = NA)
band  <- 0.5 / N
kappa <- band / (0.5 / sqrt(12))
w_policy <- setNames(rep(1 / N, N), colnames(Re))

tilt_from <- function(F, idx, reduce = identity) {
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(F), colnames(Re)), nrow(F) == length(idx))
  W <- t(vapply(seq_along(idx), function(i) {
    m  <- idx[i]
    s  <- F[i, ] / as.numeric(vol60[m - 1L, ])   # volatility units, known at m - 1
    s  <- reduce(s - mean(s))                    # relative view, then the reduction
    tl <- pmin(pmax(kappa * s, -band), band)
    w  <- w_policy + tl - mean(tl); w <- pmax(w, 0); w / sum(w)
  }, numeric(N)))
  dimnames(W) <- list(as.character(dates[idx]), colnames(Re))
  stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(W) - 1) < 1e-12), all(W >= 0))
  W
}
steps <- function(G) function(s) {                         # group averages
  if (G <= 1L) return(s * 0)
  stats::ave(s, ceiling(rank(s, ties.method = "first") * G / length(s)))
}
sign_only <- function(s) {                                 # top third +band, bottom third -band
  g <- ceiling(rank(s, ties.method = "first") * 3 / length(s))
  (band / kappa) * (as.numeric(g == 3L) - as.numeric(g == 1L))
}

cost_rate <- pm_costs_default()[sub(".*_", "", colnames(Re))]
stopifnot(!anyNA(cost_rate)); names(cost_rate) <- colnames(Re)
score_W <- function(W, idx) {
  Rm <- zoo::coredata(R)[idx, colnames(Re), drop = FALSE]
  Em <- zoo::coredata(Re)[idx, colnames(Re), drop = FALSE]
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(W), colnames(Re)), nrow(W) == nrow(Rm))
  r <- rowSums(W * Rm); e <- rowSums(W * Em)
  drifted <- W * (1 + Rm) / (1 + r)
  trade   <- abs(W[-1, , drop = FALSE] - drifted[-nrow(W), , drop = FALSE])
  cost    <- c(as.numeric(trade %*% cost_rate), 0)
  c(sharpe = sharpe_realized(r, rf_by_month[as.character(dates[idx])]),
    ce = ce_annual(e), ce_net = ce_annual(e - cost),
    turnover = 12 * mean(c(rowSums(trade) / 2, 0)))
}
```

The cell that moves needs the information coefficient. At each
out-of-sample month the regression is fit on the months before it, its fitted
values are ranked against the realized returns of those months, both in
volatility units, and the Spearman correlations are averaged: the ranking
ability an investor standing at that month could measure. @eq-27-groups then
gives the number of groups, rounded and capped at `r N %/% 2L`.

```{r}
#| label: information-coefficient
ic_of <- function(m) {
  tr <- seq.int(61L, m - 1L)
  Fhat <- vapply(colnames(Re), function(s) {
    d  <- pairs_of(s); ok <- which(!is.na(d$term) & seq_len(Tn) < m)
    b  <- stats::lm.fit(cbind(1, d$term[ok]), d$y[ok])$coefficients
    b[1] + b[2] * d$term[tr]
  }, numeric(length(tr)))
  V60 <- zoo::coredata(vol60)[tr - 1L, ]; Y60 <- zoo::coredata(Re)[tr, ]
  mean(vapply(seq_along(tr), function(i)
    stats::cor(Fhat[i, ] / V60[i, ], Y60[i, ] / V60[i, ], method = "spearman"), numeric(1)))
}
ic      <- vapply(oos, ic_of, numeric(1))
G_star  <- (2 * N * (oos - 1L) * ic^2 / (1 - ic^2))^(1 / 3)
G_rule  <- pmax(1L, pmin(N %/% 2L, as.integer(round(G_star))))

# The same coefficient on the forecasts actually made, over the register's months.
V60_oos <- zoo::coredata(vol60)[oos - 1L, ]; Y_oos <- zoo::coredata(Re)[oos, ]
ic_oos  <- mean(vapply(seq_along(oos), function(i)
  stats::cor(F_term[i, ] / V60_oos[i, ], Y_oos[i, ] / V60_oos[i, ], method = "spearman"), numeric(1)))
G_oos   <- (2 * N * length(oos) * ic_oos^2 / (1 - ic_oos^2))^(1 / 3)
stopifnot(ic_oos < min(ic))
c(ic_window_mean = mean(ic), ic_realized = ic_oos, G_star_mean = mean(G_star), G_at_realized = G_oos)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-27-granularity
#| tbl-cap: "The term-spread forecast acted on at four granularities, and at the number of groups @eq-27-groups chooses each month, over the register's months. The Sharpe ratio is the register's, gross; the certainty equivalent is annual at gamma = 5, gross and net of the per-class costs of chapter 23."
#| echo: false
cells <- list(
  every_magnitude = tilt_from(F_term, oos),
  three_groups    = tilt_from(F_term, oos, steps(3L)),
  sign_only       = tilt_from(F_term, oos, sign_only),
  equal_weight    = tilt_from(F_term, oos, function(s) s * 0))
cells$rule <- t(vapply(seq_along(oos), function(i)
  tilt_from(F_term[i, , drop = FALSE], oos[i], steps(G_rule[i]))[1, ], numeric(N)))
dimnames(cells$rule) <- dimnames(cells$every_magnitude)

lab_cells <- c(every_magnitude = "every magnitude (chapter 16)", three_groups = "three rank groups",
               sign_only = "sign only", equal_weight = "equal weight (1/N)",
               rule = "the rule: G from the information coefficient")
res_gran <- t(vapply(cells, score_W, numeric(4), idx = oos)) |>
  as.data.frame() |> tibble::rownames_to_column("cell")
stopifnot(abs(res_gran$sharpe[res_gran$cell == "equal_weight"] - sr_register("equal_weight", 60L)) < 5e-5)

res_gran |>
  dplyr::mutate(cell = lab_cells[cell], G = c("16", "3", "1", "0", paste(range(G_rule), collapse = " to "))) |>
  dplyr::transmute(cell, G, num(sharpe), pct(ce), pct(ce_net), pct(turnover, 0)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrr", col.names = c("", "dimensions", "Sharpe", "CE, gross", "CE, net", "turnover"))
```

```{r}
#| label: granularity-facts
#| include: false
g_c <- function(cell, col = "sharpe") res_gran[[col]][res_gran$cell == cell]
fc_cells  <- c("every_magnitude", "three_groups", "sign_only", "rule")
gain_sr   <- res_gran$sharpe[res_gran$cell %in% fc_cells] - g_c("equal_weight")
gain_ce   <- res_gran$ce_net[res_gran$cell %in% fc_cells] - g_c("equal_weight", "ce_net")
spread_sr <- diff(range(res_gran$sharpe[res_gran$cell %in% fc_cells]))
spread_ce <- diff(range(res_gran$ce[res_gran$cell %in% fc_cells]))
stopifnot(all(gain_sr > 0), all(gain_ce > 0), spread_sr < 0.02, spread_ce < 2e-3,
          g_c("sign_only", "turnover") > g_c("every_magnitude", "turnover"), all(G_rule >= 3L))
```

The forecast cells all stand above equal weighting, by
`r sprintf("%.3f", min(gain_sr))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", max(gain_sr))` in
Sharpe ratio and by `r sprintf("%.0f", 1e4 * min(gain_ce))` to
`r sprintf("%.0f", 1e4 * max(gain_ce))` basis points of certainty equivalent
net of costs, the order of gain @sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-application
found. Among themselves they are indistinguishable: the spread across the four
forecast cells is `r sprintf("%.3f", spread_sr)` in Sharpe ratio and
`r sprintf("%.0f", 1e4 * spread_ce)` basis points of certainty equivalent,
against a standard error of the Sharpe ratio over these months of about
`r sprintf("%.2f", se_sr)` by the formula of @lo2002. The information
coefficient on the estimation windows averages `r sprintf("%.3f", mean(ic))`,
so @eq-27-groups asks for `r paste(range(G_rule), collapse = " to ")` groups,
and the rule's cell earns `r sprintf("%.3f", g_c("rule"))`, inside the same
spread. The coefficient realized on the forecasts actually made is
`r sprintf("%.3f", ic_oos)`, lower than on any estimation window, and at that
value the formula gives `r sprintf("%.1f", G_oos)` groups: the number read
from fitted values overstates what the forecast delivers, at no visible
cost here because nothing in the granularity has one. The sign cell trades
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * g_c("sign_only", "turnover"))` a year against
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * g_c("every_magnitude", "turnover"))` for the full
vector and still matches it after costs. This is the second condition of the
theory: a forecast whose cross-sectional content is a near-common shift, the
term spread lifting every bond series together, leaves @eq-27-hard little to
discard and little to retain, and the band of @eq-16-tilt, not the
granularity, sets what the forecast is worth.

### Tuning the elastic net on the certainty equivalent

The third answer is tried on the forecaster of
@sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-implementation that lost: the elastic net of
@zou2005 on seven predictors, which chose its penalty by five-fold
cross-validated squared error on contiguous blocks, re-tuned once a year. Here
the same folds and grid of penalties serve two criteria: the pooled
out-of-fold squared error across the sixteen series, the loss of @eq-27-mse,
and the certainty equivalent of the tilt of @eq-16-tilt built from the
out-of-fold forecasts over the training months, the loss of @eq-27-loop with
the tilt as the map. The penalty is the only parameter the loop chooses; the
coefficients are refit inside `glmnet` at whichever penalty each criterion
selects.

```{r}
#| label: enet-tuning
en_vars  <- c("mom", "rev", "term", "ig", "hy", "level", "turb")
D  <- lapply(colnames(Re), pairs_of); names(D) <- colnames(Re)
ok <- stats::complete.cases(D[[1]][, en_vars])
stopifnot(all(vapply(D, function(d) identical(stats::complete.cases(d[, en_vars]), ok), logical(1))))
lam_grid <- 10^seq(-1, -5, length.out = 33)     # decreasing, as glmnet expects
Y <- zoo::coredata(Re)

tune_both <- function(m) {
  tr   <- which(ok & seq_len(Tn) < m)
  fold <- ceiling(seq_along(tr) / (length(tr) / 5))
  oof  <- array(NA_real_, c(length(tr), N, length(lam_grid)))
  for (j in seq_len(N)) {
    X <- as.matrix(D[[j]][tr, en_vars]); y <- D[[j]]$y[tr]
    for (f in 1:5) {
      i   <- fold != f
      fit <- glmnet::glmnet(X[i, ], y[i], alpha = 0.5, lambda = lam_grid)
      oof[!i, j, ] <- as.matrix(stats::predict(fit, newx = X[!i, , drop = FALSE], s = lam_grid))
    }
  }
  mse <- vapply(seq_along(lam_grid), function(k) mean((oof[, , k] - Y[tr, ])^2), numeric(1))
  ce  <- vapply(seq_along(lam_grid), function(k) {
    F <- oof[, , k]; colnames(F) <- colnames(Re)
    ce_annual(rowSums(tilt_from(F, tr) * Y[tr, ]))
  }, numeric(1))
  list(lam_mse = lam_grid[which.min(mse)], lam_ce = lam_grid[which.max(ce)],
       null_mse = which.min(mse) == 1L)     # TRUE when the null model minimizes the CV error
}

retune <- oos[(oos - oos[1]) %% 12L == 0L]
tunes  <- lapply(retune, tune_both); names(tunes) <- retune
lam_path <- tibble::tibble(date = dates[retune],
                           mse = vapply(tunes, `[[`, numeric(1), "lam_mse"),
                           ce  = vapply(tunes, `[[`, numeric(1), "lam_ce"))
null_mse <- vapply(tunes, `[[`, logical(1), "null_mse")
```

```{r}
#| label: lambda-facts
#| include: false
ce_orders <- log10(max(lam_path$ce) / min(lam_path$ce))
stopifnot(mean(null_mse) > 0.7, mean(lam_path$ce < lam_path$mse) > 0.7, ce_orders > 2)
```

The cross-validated squared error is minimized by the null model, every coefficient at zero and the forecast
equal to the training mean, in `r sum(null_mse)` of the `r length(null_mse)`
re-tunings, and by a penalty next to it in the rest: judged by @eq-27-mse,
the best elastic net on seven predictors and sixteen series is no elastic
net, the conclusion @sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-application reached by a
longer route. The certainty-equivalent criterion selects a smaller penalty in
`r sum(lam_path$ce < lam_path$mse)` of the `r nrow(lam_path)` re-tunings and
wanders over `r sprintf("%.0f", ce_orders)` orders of magnitude from one year
to the next, which is what a criterion estimated with the noise of a Sharpe
ratio looks like when the surface it searches is flat.

```{r}
#| label: enet-forecast
fc_en <- function(which_lam) {
  lam <- NA_real_
  out <- vapply(oos, function(m) {
    if (m %in% retune) lam <<- tunes[[as.character(m)]][[which_lam]]
    tr <- which(ok & seq_len(Tn) < m)
    vapply(seq_len(N), function(j) {
      fit <- glmnet::glmnet(as.matrix(D[[j]][tr, en_vars]), D[[j]]$y[tr], alpha = 0.5, lambda = lam_grid)
      as.numeric(stats::predict(fit, newx = as.matrix(D[[j]][m, en_vars]), s = lam))
    }, numeric(1))
  }, numeric(N))
  out <- t(out); dimnames(out) <- list(as.character(dates[oos]), colnames(Re)); out
}
F_mse  <- fc_en("lam_mse")
F_ce   <- fc_en("lam_ce")
F_mean <- vapply(colnames(Re), function(s)
  vapply(oos, function(m) mean(Y[seq_len(m - 1L), s]), numeric(1)), numeric(length(oos)))
dimnames(F_mean) <- dimnames(F_mse)

r2_os <- function(F) 1 - sum((Y[oos, ] - F)^2) / sum((Y[oos, ] - F_mean)^2)
res_train <- tibble::tibble(
  forecast = c("elastic net, tuned on squared error", "elastic net, tuned on the certainty equivalent",
               "historical mean"),
  mse  = c(mean((Y[oos, ] - F_mse)^2), mean((Y[oos, ] - F_ce)^2), mean((Y[oos, ] - F_mean)^2)),
  r2os = c(r2_os(F_mse), r2_os(F_ce), 0)) |>
  dplyr::bind_cols(dplyr::bind_rows(score_W(tilt_from(F_mse, oos), oos),
                                    score_W(tilt_from(F_ce, oos), oos),
                                    score_W(tilt_from(F_mean, oos), oos)))
```

```{r}
#| label: training-facts
#| include: false
g_t <- function(i, col) res_train[[col]][i]
turn_x <- g_t(2, "turnover") / g_t(1, "turnover")
stopifnot(g_t(2, "mse") > g_t(1, "mse"),            # the decision-trained forecast has the worse MSE
          g_t(2, "sharpe") > g_t(1, "sharpe"),      # and the better portfolio
          g_t(2, "ce_net") > g_t(1, "ce_net"),
          turn_x > 2, g_t(2, "sharpe") - g_t(1, "sharpe") < se_sr)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-27-training
#| tbl-cap: "The same elastic net tuned on two losses, scored over the register's months: pooled mean squared error of the forecast and its out-of-sample R-squared against the expanding mean, then the Sharpe ratio, certainty equivalent and turnover of the tilt built on it."
#| echo: false
res_train |>
  dplyr::transmute(forecast, num(1e4 * mse, 2), sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * r2os),
                   num(sharpe), pct(ce), pct(ce_net), pct(turnover, 0)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrrr",
        col.names = c("", "MSE (x 10^4)", "R²OS", "Sharpe", "CE, gross", "CE, net", "turnover"))
```

@tbl-27-training is the result the chapter was built to show. The forecast
tuned on the certainty equivalent has the worse mean squared error, an
out-of-sample $R^2$ of `r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * g_t(2, "r2os"))` against
the expanding mean where the squared-error forecast has
`r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * g_t(1, "r2os"))`, and the better portfolio: a
Sharpe ratio of `r sprintf("%.3f", g_t(2, "sharpe"))` against
`r sprintf("%.3f", g_t(1, "sharpe"))` and a certainty equivalent net of costs
of `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * g_t(2, "ce_net"))` against
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * g_t(1, "ce_net"))`,
`r sprintf("%.0f", 1e4 * (g_t(2, "ce_net") - g_t(1, "ce_net")))` basis points a
year. Trained on the loss the decision bears, the forecaster gives up accuracy
in the directions the optimizer does not use and keeps it where the tilt
acts, @eq-27-gls in a case where no closed form exists. Two qualifications
belong beside the number: the decision-trained net turns the portfolio over
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * g_t(2, "turnover"))` a year,
`r sprintf("%.0f", turn_x)` times the
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * g_t(1, "turnover"))` of the squared-error net,
because the penalty it chooses lets the forecasts move; and the Sharpe-ratio
advantage of `r sprintf("%.3f", g_t(2, "sharpe") - g_t(1, "sharpe"))` is inside
the standard error of `r sprintf("%.2f", se_sr)`. The prediction is confirmed
in sign and not established in significance, which on `r length(oos)` months
is as much as any forecast comparison in this book can say.

## What Each Answer Buys {#sec-27-decision-aware-forecasting-application}

```{r}
#| label: fig-27-scoreboard
#| fig-cap: "Every rule of this chapter and every line of the register, scored on the same months with sixty-month estimation windows, in the register's Sharpe ratio, from one data frame. The dashed line is equal weighting."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.62
board <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  sweep_all |> dplyr::filter(window == 60L) |>
    dplyr::transmute(label = paste0(label, " (register)"), sharpe, kind = "register"),
  tibble::tibble(label = c("tangency, Bayes-Stein", "tangency, corrected mean"),
                 sharpe = c(g_m("bayes_stein", 60L), g_m("corrected", 60L)), kind = "corrected mean"),
  tibble::tibble(label = paste("term tilt,", c("every magnitude", "three groups", "sign only", "rule")),
                 sharpe = c(g_c("every_magnitude"), g_c("three_groups"), g_c("sign_only"), g_c("rule")),
                 kind = "granularity"),
  tibble::tibble(label = c("elastic net, squared error", "elastic net, certainty equivalent"),
                 sharpe = c(g_t(1, "sharpe"), g_t(2, "sharpe")), kind = "training loop")
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(label = stats::reorder(label, sharpe))

ggplot2::ggplot(board, ggplot2::aes(sharpe, label, colour = kind)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = sr_register("equal_weight", 60L), linetype = "22",
                      linewidth = 0.35, colour = tidyaa_colors[["ink_soft"]]) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_tidyaa() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "out-of-sample Sharpe ratio, sixty-month windows", y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: board-facts
#| include: false
best_fc  <- board |> dplyr::filter(kind != "register") |> dplyr::slice_max(sharpe, n = 1)
best_reg <- board |> dplyr::filter(kind == "register") |> dplyr::slice_max(sharpe, n = 1)
stopifnot(best_reg$sharpe > best_fc$sharpe, sr_register("min_variance", 60L) > best_fc$sharpe,
          best_fc$label == "tangency, corrected mean",
          g_t(2, "sharpe") > g_c("every_magnitude"), g_t(2, "sharpe") > g_m("bayes_stein", 60L))
gain_a <- g_m("corrected", 60L) - g_m("sample", 60L)
gain_b <- g_c("every_magnitude") - sr_register("equal_weight", 60L)
gain_c <- g_t(2, "sharpe") - g_t(1, "sharpe")
```

@fig-27-scoreboard puts the three answers on one axis with the register of
@sec-25-backtesting-application. In the Sharpe ratio added to the rule it
corrects, the first answer buys most: the corrected mean lifts the
sixty-month tangency portfolio by `r sprintf("%.2f", gain_a)`, from the
register's `r sprintf("%.3f", g_m("sample", 60L))` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", g_m("corrected", 60L))`, at 120 months by
`r sprintf("%.2f", g_m("corrected", 120L) - g_m("sample", 120L))`, and the
corrected tangency portfolio is the best forecast-based rule in the figure.
The third answer buys `r sprintf("%.2f", gain_c)` over the same forecaster
tuned on squared error, which makes the decision-trained net the best of the
tilts at `r sprintf("%.3f", g_t(2, "sharpe"))`,
`r sprintf("%.0f", 1e4 * (g_t(2, "ce_net") - g_c("equal_weight", "ce_net")))`
basis points of net certainty equivalent above equal weighting. The second
answer buys the `r sprintf("%.2f", gain_b)` that the term spread was already
worth in @sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-application and nothing beyond it. In
certainty equivalent the first two change places: the training loop adds
`r sprintf("%.0f", 1e4 * (g_t(2, "ce_net") - g_t(1, "ce_net")))` basis points
net to its forecaster where the corrected mean adds
`r sprintf("%.0f", 1e4 * (g_m("corrected", 60L, "ce") - g_m("sample", 60L, "ce")))`
to a fully invested tangency rule whose length is not its own to choose.

Each fails somewhere. The corrected mean does not beat the rules that use no mean: the register's
minimum variance stands at `r sprintf("%.3f", sr_register("min_variance", 60L))`
and its best line, `r sub(" \\(register\\)$", "", as.character(best_reg$label))`,
at `r sprintf("%.3f", best_reg$sharpe)`, above every forecast-based rule in
the figure, and on `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * share_gmv(60L))` of the
sixty-month windows the correction concedes the point by collapsing onto
minimum variance itself; the covariance channel of @eq-08-kz it leaves
untouched is where that rule's advantage lives. Granularity fails to matter:
four ways of acting on the term spread land within
`r sprintf("%.3f", spread_sr)` of one another, the rule's choice of
`r paste(range(G_rule), collapse = " to ")` groups rests on an information
coefficient measured in sample that the realized forecasts do not reach, and
with sixteen assets and a band of `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * band)` percentage
points there is too little cross-section for @eq-27-hard to decide anything.
And the training loop, the answer that generalizes furthest, is the one
whose own prediction is only partially borne out: it delivers a forecast
with a worse squared error and a better portfolio, but it chooses its penalty
from a criterion so noisy that the choice moves by orders of magnitude
between years, trades `r sprintf("%.0f", turn_x)` times as much, and leaves a
Sharpe-ratio gain the sample cannot distinguish from zero. The decision loss
is the right teacher and a far noisier one than squared error.

For the plug-in rules of @sec-09-mean-variance-application and
@sec-08-estimation-error-application the reading is short. The sixty-month
tangency portfolio's `r sprintf("%.3f", g_m("sample", 60L))` was never the
price of using an estimated mean; it was the price of using the sample mean,
and @eq-27-corrector recovers
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * gain_a / (sr_register("min_variance", 60L) - g_m("sample", 60L)))`
of the distance to minimum variance without touching the covariance matrix,
with a constant that needed no tuning. What remains is the covariance
matrix's share, which @sec-26-forecast-error-cost-theory separates from the
mean's, and the part no estimator can recover: on this market the level
direction that minimum variance trades carries most of what there is to
earn, and the decision-aware forecaster changes which loss that arithmetic
is done in, not the arithmetic. @sec-28-robustness-theory asks what to do when the model behind
the loss is itself in doubt, and the resampled frontiers of
@sec-28-robustness-application put the same estimation error back on the
picture of @sec-09-mean-variance-application.

## Key Takeaways {.unnumbered}

- A mean-variance investor pays for forecast error in the metric
  $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}$, not the identity (@eq-27-decision): on the
  sixteen classes the same squared error costs
  $10^{`r sprintf("%.1f", log10(cost_bottom / cost_top))`}$ times more in
  the least volatile direction than in the most [@salcher2026; @elmachtoub2022].
- Shrinking the sample mean toward the grand mean in estimated risk units has
  an exact risk; the best constant is $(N - 3)(T - 1)/(T - N + 2)$, a
  function of $N$ and $T$ alone, and the corrected mean dominates the sample
  mean whenever $T > N$ [@stoeckl2026means; @james1961; @stein1981]. On
  sixty-month windows it lifts the tangency portfolio's Sharpe ratio from
  `r sprintf("%.2f", g_m("sample", 60L))` to
  `r sprintf("%.2f", g_m("corrected", 60L))` and collapses onto minimum
  variance, which stays ahead, in
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * share_gmv(60L))` of the windows.
- Every dimension of a forecast acted on costs $1/T$ whatever it carries, so
  the familiar rules are cells of a granularity grid and the number of rank
  groups worth forming is $(2NT\rho^2/(1 - \rho^2))^{1/3}$ from the
  information coefficient [@salcher2026less; @cattaneo2020]. On the term
  spread every granularity earns the same few basis points: the band of the
  tilt, not its resolution, sets the value.
- Tuning the elastic net's penalty on the certainty equivalent of the tilt it
  implies instead of on squared error gives a forecast with a worse
  $R^2_{\text{OS}}$ and a better portfolio,
  `r sprintf("%.0f", 1e4 * (g_t(2, "ce_net") - g_t(1, "ce_net")))` basis
  points net a year, inside the sampling error of the Sharpe ratio and at
  `r sprintf("%.0f", turn_x)` times the turnover [@brandt2009; @bertsimas2020].
- None of the three answers beats the register's rules that use no mean. The
  correction prices the mean channel; the covariance channel of @eq-08-kz is
  where the rest of the plug-in rule's loss lives.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Run the sixty-month backtest of @tbl-27-means with the zero target in
   place of the grand mean. The long-only tangency rule's Sharpe ratio should
   equal the sample mean's exactly, except on windows where the factor is
   zero; verify both halves and count the exceptions. Then hold the
   unconstrained position
   $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}/\gamma$ on the
   sample mean, the zero target and the grand mean, and compare their
   realized certainty equivalents at $\gamma = 5$ with @eq-08-kz in mind.
2. @eq-27-risk says the risk is below $N/T$ for every constant in
   $(0, 2c_f)$. Simulate two thousand sixty-month samples from the
   full-sample moments and measure the squared RAFE of the corrected mean at
   $c \in \{c_f/2,\, c_f,\, 1.5\,c_f,\, 2.5\,c_f\}$. Which lies above $N/T$?
   Then run the rolling backtest at the same constants: does the tangency
   rule's Sharpe ratio move monotonically with $c$, and what does the answer
   say about the positive part?
3. Double the band of @eq-16-tilt to $\delta = 1/N$ and recompute
   @tbl-27-granularity. Does granularity begin to matter once the forecast
   may move the weights further, and does the sign cell still match the full
   vector after costs?
4. The information coefficient in @tbl-27-granularity is measured on fitted
   values. Replace it, from the second out-of-sample year on, with the
   trailing coefficient of the forecasts actually made, and recompute the
   number of groups month by month. How often does the rule now hold $1/N$?
